analysis.one_liner: Lets doctors own and expand hospitals they refer their own patients to, dropping limits and disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors, has sat untouched in two House committees since April 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare's physician self-referral law ('Stark law') generally bars doctors from sending Medicare patients to hospitals they own, with a narrow exception for hospitals that existed in 2010 that don't expand, don't grow ownership, and disclose their ownership to patients. This bill wipes out those conditions, so physicians could own hospitals, open new ones converted from surgery centers, expand operating rooms and beds, and increase their ownership stakes while still referring their own Medicare patients there. It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Physician-investors who own, or want to own, hospitals. They could build or buy in, expand capacity, raise their ownership percentages, and convert surgery centers into full hospitals, all while keeping the ability to refer their own patients to those facilities under Medicare.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the 2010-era conditions that physician-owned hospitals must meet to qualify for the Stark law exception, including caps on expanding beds, operating rooms, and procedure rooms and limits on growing ownership stakes.

Removes the requirements that physician-owned hospitals disclose their ownership to patients, the public, and Medicare, and that they disclose physician availability and arrange alternatives when needed.
Ends the bar on converting ambulatory surgical centers into physician-owned hospitals after March 23, 2010, reopening a pathway for new physician-owned facilities.
Repeals parallel conditions that applied to rural providers, letting them invest in hospitals they refer to without the extra criteria.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare and its taxpayers, and patients more broadly. Self-referral gives doctors a financial stake in the scans, surgeries, and admissions they order, a setup Medicare's law was written to curb; community hospitals also lose the profitable surgical cases that help fund care for sicker and uninsured patients.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the disclosure requirement that physician-owned hospitals tell patients who owns the facility, so a patient referred to a hospital would no longer be guaranteed notice that the referring doctor profits from the facility.

The bill removes the limits on expansion and on raising ownership stakes, which by design had kept physician self-referral from growing; self-referral gives physicians a personal financial incentive in the volume of tests and procedures they order, which is the conflict of interest the Stark law exists to address.
It would again allow converting ambulatory surgical centers into physician-owned hospitals, expanding the universe of facilities where the referring physician and the facility share a profit motive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to a specific set of physician-investors who would get broader rights to own and profit from facilities they control patient flow into. The costs fall on the public side of the ledger: higher Medicare utilization and spending where self-referral grows, and community hospitals losing the well-paid cases that subsidize unprofitable care. Any benefit to patients through added capacity or choice is speculative, and the bill's own repeal of patient disclosure requirements removes one of the main safeguards meant to let patients judge the conflict for themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It went to two House committees the day it was introduced and has had no hearings, no vote, and no movement since.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the bill on April 24, 2025; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
Neither committee has taken further action on the bill since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: the existing limits on physician self-referral remain in force, and physician-investors have gained nothing yet. The main effect of the inaction is that the status quo holds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; existing self-referral limits stand

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee.

sides.party_line_note: No other member signed on and no vote occurred, so no partisan pattern is visible; the record shows only the referral and zero cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would let them own, expand, and convert hospitals and drop disclosure rules, while keeping the right to refer their own Medicare patients to facilities they profit from. Their gain comes from the self-referral arrangement Medicare's law was designed to restrict.

They would face new competition from physician-owned facilities for lucrative surgical and imaging cases while continuing to handle emergency, charity, and complex care. Their interest in keeping the current limits runs with patients' interest in restraining self-referral.
The repeal reopens the pathway to convert a surgery center into a physician-owned hospital, a route open to their investor-physician owners.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action in months, and referral to two committees, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress; bills that sit without cosponsors or hearings this long typically die when the session ends.
